summary: Pulakeshin I made Vatapi (Badami) his fortress-capital in 543, and his grandson Pulakeshin II (c. 609–642) became master of most of the Deccan, defeating the northern emperor Harsha and founding a branch at Vengi in the east. The Pallavas sacked Badami in 642, but Vikramaditya I restored the kingdom in 655, and his successors raided Kanchipuram and adorned Pattadakal with temples. In 753 the Rashtrakuta vassal Dantidurga overthrew Kirtivarman II and ended the line.
details: Pulakeshin I, a chief of the Chalukya family, made Vatapi (modern Badami) his capital in 543, choosing a site guarded by sandstone cliffs in northern Karnataka. Pulakeshin I fought the Kadambas of Banavasi, and his sons Kirtivarman I (566–597) and Mangalesha (597–609) went on enlarging the kingdom. In the cliffs above Badami the Chalukyas carved cave temples to Shiva and Vishnu; an inscription in one of them, in Kannada, is dated 578 and attributed to Mangalesha. These caves are among the earliest monuments of the Chalukya style of architecture.

Kirtivarman I had died while his son Pulakeshin was still young, so the throne passed to his brother Mangalesha. When Mangalesha tried to secure the succession for his own son, Pulakeshin fought and overthrew him, taking power around 609 (estimates range from 609 to 611). The new king first crushed rebels and then won back Banavasi from the Kadambas and forced the submission of the Alupas, the Gangas of Talakad and the Mauryas of the Konkan coast. Within a few years most of the western Deccan obeyed Badami.

Pulakeshin II then turned east. Around 616 he defeated the remnants of the Vishnukundina kingdom in coastal Andhra and also claimed Kalinga and Dakshina Kosala. In 621 he made his brother Kubja Vishnuvardhana viceroy of Vengi, the rich delta land between the Krishna and Godavari rivers. The kingdom now stretched from the Arabian Sea to the Bay of Bengal. After Pulakeshin's death the Vengi viceroyalty became independent, and Vishnuvardhana's descendants, the Eastern Chalukyas, ruled there for some four centuries.

In the north, Harshavardhana of Kannauj had built an empire across the Ganges plain and sought to push south. Pulakeshin II met him on the Narmada river and defeated him, probably around 618–619, though some scholars date the war to the 630s. The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang heard of the battle, and later Chalukya and Rashtrakuta records proudly recalled it. Pulakeshin's inscriptions also claim the submission of the Latas, Malavas and Gurjaras. The Narmada became the frontier between the two greatest Indian kingdoms of the age.

In 634 the court poet Ravikirti composed a Sanskrit praise poem for Pulakeshin II, carved in stone at Aihole, an early Chalukya temple town near Badami. The inscription lists the king's victories over the Kadambas, Gangas, Mauryas of the Konkan, Latas, Malavas and Gurjaras, his defeat of Harsha and his wars against the Pallavas. It is the main source for the reign and a landmark of classical Sanskrit poetry. At this moment the Chalukya kingdom was at its height, holding most of the Deccan.

The Chinese Buddhist pilgrim Xuanzang travelled through India in the 630s and 640s, and around 641–642 he passed through the Chalukya lands. He described a powerful and prosperous kingdom whose ruler was feared by his neighbours and commanded a large army, including war elephants. The Arab historian al-Tabari also reports diplomatic contact between Pulakeshin and the Persian king Khosrow II. Yet the long war with the Pallavas in the south was about to turn against the Chalukyas.

Pulakeshin II had invaded the Pallava kingdom of Kanchipuram several times with mixed results. Around 642 the Pallava king Narasimhavarman I struck back, marched deep into Chalukya territory and captured Vatapi itself. Pulakeshin is presumed to have been killed in the fighting. The Pallavas occupied Badami for about thirteen years, a humiliation the Pallavas long celebrated. The Chalukya kingdom fell into confusion, with several of Pulakeshin's sons ruling parts of it in turn, and the eastern viceroyalty at Vengi went its own way.

Pulakeshin's son Vikramaditya I rebuilt Chalukya power. By 655 he had expelled the Pallavas from Badami, brought rebellious vassals back under control and reunited the kingdom; he took the title Rajamalla. He ruled until 680 and carried the war back into Pallava country. His son Vinayaditya (680–696) and grandson Vijayaditya (696–733) kept the restored kingdom strong. Vijayaditya's long reign was a peaceful and prosperous time, remembered above all for temple building.

Vijayaditya's long reign (696–733) was a prosperous time, remembered for its temple building. The Chalukyas built a group of grand stone temples at Pattadakal, on the Malaprabha river near Badami, and the Sangameshvara temple there dates to about 725. Later kings and queens added more, including the Galaganatha temple of about 740 and the Virupaksha and Mallikarjuna temples of about 740–745. Pattadakal, with Aihole and Badami, became the showcase of Chalukya wealth and devotion in stone.

In the early 8th century the armies of the Umayyad Caliphate, based in Sind, raided deep into western India. Around 739 an Arab force from Sind advanced into southern Gujarat, the Lata country governed by a branch of the Chalukya family based at Navsari. The governor, Avanijanashraya Pulakeshin, defeated it and drove it out. The victory helped stop the Arab advance into the Deccan, and the Chalukya king Vikramaditya II honoured him with the title Avanijanashraya, 'refuge of the people of the earth'.

Vikramaditya II (c. 733–746) carried the old feud with the Pallavas to its climax. After 734 he invaded their kingdom, defeated Nandivarman II and entered Kanchipuram; the Narwan plates of 741 or 742 are the earliest record of the campaign. He is said to have taken the city three times in all. Rather than plunder it, he returned treasure to its temples, recorded in a Kannada inscription in the Kailasanatha temple. To mark his victory his queens built the Virupaksha and Mallikarjuna temples at Pattadakal.

Kirtivarman II succeeded his father in 746, but the Chalukya kingdom had been weakened by decades of war with the Pallavas, and its northern vassals were growing strong. One of them, the Rashtrakuta chief Dantidurga, ruled lands in the northern Deccan around Ellora. In 753 he defeated Kirtivarman II, according to his Samangadh copper-plate grant, and took over the northern Chalukya lands. Kirtivarman held on in the south for a short time, but the Badami Chalukya line was finished, and the Rashtrakutas became the new masters of the Deccan.
